scenes.title: Watch the whole story first

beats.text: Consider a heavy box resting on a rough ramp. A worker pushes it up the slope with a force P, along the ramp... but the box stays exactly where it is.
Push gently, and the box wants to slip down. Friction grips it, acting up the slope, and holds it still.
Push harder. The box still does not move... but now it wants to slip up. So friction has switched, and acts down the slope.
Push harder still, and the box is on the very point of sliding up. Friction is at its maximum. Any more, and it moves.
So there is a smallest push, and a largest push, that keep the box still. Those two numbers are today’s question.

scenes.title: When is friction at its limit?

beats.text: Back on a flat floor for a moment. No push, no friction: the block simply sits.
Push with twenty newtons, and friction pushes back with exactly twenty. It matches the demand, so the block stays still.
Friction can only grow up to a limit: f is less than or equal to mu R.
When the push reaches that limit, the block is on the point of sliding. That is limiting equilibrium, and only then is f equal to mu R.
beats.ink: on the point of sliding: f = μR

beats.text: So a block at rest does not always have maximum friction. Only write f equals mu R when the block is about to slip.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The full question. A block of mass four kilograms rests on a rough plane inclined at thirty degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is zero point two five. Take g as ten.
A force P acts on the block up the plane, along the line of greatest slope. The block is in equilibrium.
Find the least value of P, and the greatest value of P, for which the block stays at rest.
Before any working: for the least push, which way is the block about to slip... and which way does friction act? Take a moment.

scenes.title: Resolve, then the friction limit

beats.text: First the weight: four times ten, forty newtons, straight down. Draw its triangle against the slope.
Into the slope: m g cos theta. Forty cos thirty is twenty root three, about thirty-four point six newtons.
Down the slope: m g sine theta. Forty sine thirty is twenty newtons.
Perpendicular to the slope nothing moves, and P has no part that way. So R minus m g cos theta equals zero.
R is twenty root three, about thirty-four point six newtons.
The most friction the plane can give: f max equals mu R.
Zero point two five times thirty-four point six... about eight point six six newtons. Keep that number; both answers use it.

scenes.title: The least push

beats.text: The least push. The block is on the point of sliding down, so friction acts up the slope... at its maximum, eight point six six.
Along the slope the forces balance. Up the slope: P plus f max. Down the slope: m g sine theta.
So P plus eight point six six minus twenty equals zero.
The least push is twenty minus eight point six six: about eleven point three newtons.
Friction helps here: it carries eight point six six, so the push can be smaller.

scenes.title: The greatest push

beats.text: Now the greatest push. The block is on the point of sliding up, so friction switches and acts down the slope, still at eight point six six.
Balance along the slope again. Up: P. Down: friction, plus m g sine theta.
P minus eight point six six minus twenty equals zero.
The greatest push is twenty plus eight point six six: about twenty-eight point seven newtons.
Same block, same limit. Only the friction direction changed, and the answer moved from eleven point three to twenty-eight point seven.

scenes.title: Between the two limits

beats.text: Any push between eleven point three and twenty-eight point seven newtons holds the block. In that range friction is less than its maximum, so never write f equals mu R there.
What if P were exactly twenty newtons? Along the slope, P minus m g sine theta equals f. Twenty minus twenty... friction is zero. The push alone balances the weight.
Know when friction is at its limit.
